chapters.title: Who really creates money: banks, the Fed and the Treasury
chapters.kicker: Bank loans are only one door. The Fed, the Treasury and even your tax payment move money between two floors, and only one of them is money you can spend.

blocks.label: In 60 seconds
items: Money lives on two floors. Upstairs, banks and the Treasury hold accounts at the Federal Reserve. Downstairs, you and every business hold bank deposits. You can only spend the downstairs kind.
Banks create most new downstairs money when they lend, and they also create it when they buy a bond or anything else from someone who is not a bank.

The Fed creates upstairs money, called reserves, every time it buys a bond. Whether new downstairs money appears too depends on who sold the bond: a bank (no) or a pension fund or other nonbank (yes).
The Treasury moves money between the floors. Selling bonds and collecting taxes pulls deposits up into its Fed account. Spending pushes them back down.
So money is not created only by bank loans. In 2020 and 2021 the Treasury and the Fed together created most of the $5.45 trillion rise in bank deposits.
The Fed is not allowed to buy new bonds straight from the Treasury. It must buy in the open market, through 25 primary dealers.
In short: banks are the everyday printer. The government and the Fed together are the emergency printer, and when both switch it on, as in 2020, it is bigger than anything the banks do.

From 1971 to 2026, bank loans grew about $13.79T and the Fed's bonds about $6.43T: two thirds downstairs, one third upstairs, with the upstairs third arriving in two bursts, 2008 to 2014 and 2020 to 2021.

items.d: Banks' own accounts at the Fed. Upstairs money. About $2.96 trillion in October 2026. Only banks and a few institutions can hold them.
The money in your bank account. Downstairs money, a promise from your bank. About $19.6 trillion at US commercial banks.
The government's checking account at the Fed. About $952 billion in late October 2026. Money in it is out of public hands.
One of 25 big dealers that must bid at every Treasury auction and that trade directly with the Fed.
The market where bonds already issued change hands. The only place the Fed may buy Treasuries.

blocks.text: Chapter 6 showed that a bank loan creates a deposit. That is the most common way money is born, but not the only one. This chapter finishes the picture. It adds the Fed, the Treasury and the dealers in between, and shows exactly which moves create money you can spend and which only shuffle money that banks use among themselves.
Two floors of money

Picture the dollar system as a building with two floors. Upstairs are the Fed's books. Banks hold reserves there, the Treasury holds its account there, and money funds can park cash there overnight. Downstairs are the public's books: deposits at banks, plus paper cash. When you pay rent or buy groceries, you move downstairs money. Banks settle with each other upstairs.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Think of a big market hall. Upstairs is the wholesale floor, where only licensed traders deal, and they settle in special tokens issued by the hall's owner, the Fed. Downstairs is the shop floor, where everyone shops with receipts issued by the traders, which are bank deposits. Some deals happen only upstairs, between traders and the owner. Some happen only downstairs. And some go through the staircase and change the amount of receipts on the shop floor. This chapter is a guide to the staircase.

blocks.caption: Upstairs: reserves, the Treasury's account and cash parked at the Fed. Downstairs: deposits and cash held by the public. Arrows show which moves cross the staircase.

rows: Cash parked by money funds at the Fed (overnight reverse repo)
What the Fed holds against all this: Treasuries and mortgage bonds
Paper cash (a Fed liability that the public holds)
M2, the broad measure of the public's money

blocks.q: Can a family spend bank reserves at a shop?
blocks.a: No. Reserves are accounts at the Fed that only banks and a few institutions hold. A family spends deposits or cash. Reserves only matter to the family when a move also changes deposits.

blocks.text: Step 1. Banks create deposits, and not only by lending

When a bank lends you $100, it adds a $100 loan to its assets and a $100 deposit to its debts at the same moment. New downstairs money appears. When you repay, both disappear. That is Chapter 6. The second way is less known. When a bank buys a $100 bond from a pension fund, it pays by crediting the fund's account with a new $100 deposit. No loan was made, but money was created all the same. When a bank sells a bond to a nonbank, money is destroyed.
Whenever a bank makes a loan, it simultaneously creates a matching deposit in the borrower's bank account, thereby creating new money.
blocks.by: Bank of England, Money creation in the modern economy, 2014

items: A bank lends $100 to a household: the household's deposit rises $100. New money.
The household repays: the deposit and the loan both shrink $100. Money destroyed.
A bank buys a $100 bond from a pension fund: the fund's deposit rises $100. New money without a loan.
Upstairs, nothing changed in total. Reserves only move between banks when the money is spent at another bank.

blocks.q: Your bank buys a building from a developer for $1 million and pays into the developer's account at the same bank. Did the money supply change?
blocks.a: Yes, it rose by $1 million. The bank gained an asset (the building) and a new deposit liability (the developer's balance). Any purchase by a bank from a nonbank creates a deposit.

blocks.text: Step 2. The Fed creates reserves when it buys, and the seller decides the rest

The Fed holds $4.57 trillion of Treasuries. It got them by buying in the open market from the 25 primary dealers, paying with reserves it creates on the spot, and by rolling over bonds as they mature. That is real money creation, but upstairs. Whether it reaches downstairs depends on who sold the bond in the end.

cols: Who sells the bond to the Fed
rows: No change. The bank swapped a bond for reserves.
A pension fund, insurer, money fund or foreign investor
Up $100. The seller's bank gets reserves and credits the seller's deposit.
A dealer selling from its own stock
Up $100 at first. If the dealer uses the cash to repay a loan from a bank, the deposit disappears again.

blocks.caption: Two paths for the same $100 purchase. From a bank, only reserves rise. From a pension fund, reserves and deposits both rise.

blocks.text: When the Federal Reserve purchases securities from a nonbank seller, it creates new bank deposits.
blocks.by: Castro, Cavallo and Zarutskie, Federal Reserve FEDS Notes, 2022

blocks.text: The primary dealer in the middle is only the pipe. Most primary dealers are the securities arms of big banks, and many act for customers. To know whether a Fed purchase added money you can spend, follow the cash to whoever holds it at the end. In 2020 to 2022 much of the selling came from nonbanks, which is why quantitative easing then added deposits as well as reserves.

blocks.q: The Fed buys $1 billion of Treasuries, and the sellers turn out to be three banks. How much new money can the public spend?
blocks.a: None directly. Bank reserves rose $1 billion, which is upstairs money. Public deposits change only if the sellers are nonbanks, or later when banks spend or lend.

blocks.text: Step 3. The Treasury moves money between the floors

The Treasury keeps its account at the Fed, upstairs. When a fund buys a new Treasury bond at auction, the fund's deposit falls, its bank's reserves fall, and the Treasury's account rises. Money has gone upstairs. When the Treasury pays a Social Security check, the reverse happens: the account falls, and the retiree's deposit and the bank's reserves rise. Taxes work like an auction: deposits go up the stairs. You can watch it happen. In the week to 21 October 2026 the Treasury's account rose $69 billion, and bank reserves fell $60 billion.

blocks.caption: Auctions and taxes lift money into the Treasury's account at the Fed. Spending sends it back down. A deficit means more goes down than comes up.

blocks.text: So does a budget deficit create money? It depends on who buys the new bonds. In fiscal 2026 the deficit was $1.99 trillion.

rows: Households and funds, paying from their deposits
None overall. The deposits taken at auction come back when the Treasury spends. The buyers now hold a bond instead.
Deposits rise. Banks pay with reserves, the spending lands in someone's account.
The Fed, indirectly, buying later from nonbanks
Deposits and reserves both rise. This is the legal route to printing money for a deficit.
Money funds using cash parked at the Fed
Deposits rise. Cash that was upstairs comes down when the Treasury spends.

blocks.q: The Treasury runs a $100 deficit and a pension fund buys the whole $100 bond with its bank deposit. What happens to deposits?
blocks.a: Nothing overall. The fund's deposit fell $100 at the auction, and the Treasury's spending added $100 to someone else's deposit. The private sector holds $100 more in bonds, not more money.

blocks.text: Step 4. Drains, new pipes and the Fed's own bills

items: The overnight reverse repo facility: money funds can lend cash to the Fed overnight. While it sits there, it is out of the banks. It held about $1.8 trillion in March 2022. By October 2026 the domestic part was $0.3 billion, so this drain is empty.
The Treasury General Account: every rise drains reserves and often deposits, every fall adds them back.

Stablecoins: buying a dollar token moves your deposit to the issuer, who buys Treasury bills. Bank deposits do not grow, and if the bill comes from a bank or the Treasury, they shrink. The token is a new private dollar outside M2.
Interest on reserves: the Fed pays banks interest by creating new reserves, about $115 billion a year at current rates (desk estimate). Deposits grow only if banks pass it on.

Fed profits and losses: when the Fed earns more than it pays, it sends the profit to the Treasury. Since 2022 it has paid more than it earns and owes itself $232.7 billion before payments restart. The 'taxes go to the Fed's owners' story has it backwards.

blocks.q: A money fund pulls $50 billion out of the Fed's reverse repo facility to buy new Treasury bills, and the Treasury spends the cash. What happens downstairs?
blocks.a: Deposits rise about $50 billion. The cash was upstairs at the Fed, it passed through the Treasury's account, and the spending landed in public accounts.

blocks.text: Why the Fed cannot just buy from the Treasury

Section 14 of the Federal Reserve Act says US government bonds may be bought "only in the open market". Congress added that rule in 1935 so that the Treasury would have to face market buyers and could not finance itself at its own central bank. A wartime exception from 1942 allowed up to $5 billion of direct purchases. It was renewed several times, last in 1979, and lapsed in 1981. The Fed can still roll over bonds it already owns by taking new ones at auction, which gives the Treasury no new cash.

A ban on direct buying is not a ban on financing. From 1942 to 1951 the Fed promised to keep bill rates at 0.375% and long bond yields under 2.5%, buying whatever the market sold at those prices. That financed the war debt cheaply without a single direct purchase. The Treasury-Fed Accord of 4 March 1951 ended the deal.
Putting sizes on it

blocks.caption: Every channel that creates or destroys the public's deposits, with rough sizes for the latest year and for 2020 to 2021.

rows: small, apart from a short burst in early 2020
$5.9T of new Treasury debt, 72% bought by the Fed and banks

blocks.text: In an ordinary year, bank lending is the biggest engine. In the pandemic it was the government and the central bank: the Treasury spent borrowed money straight into household accounts, and the Fed and banks bought most of the new bonds, so nothing drained the deposits back. M2 rose 41% in two years, from $15.5 trillion in February 2020 to $21.8 trillion in February 2022.

blocks.myth: All money is created by banks making loans.
blocks.reality: Loans are the main channel most years, but banks also create money when they buy securities, the Fed creates reserves whenever it buys and deposits when the seller is a nonbank, and Treasury spending adds deposits unless the public funded it from its own accounts. In 2020 to 2021 the Treasury and Fed channel created most new deposits.

blocks.myth: The Fed prints money and hands it to the government.
blocks.reality: The Fed may not lend to the Treasury or buy at auction. It buys bonds from dealers in the open market and pays the sellers. That holds down yields and can turn bonds held by the public into deposits, which finances deficits indirectly. Its profits go back to the Treasury, and since 2022 it has been running losses.

blocks.text: So who is printing? The everyday printer and the emergency printer

Put all of this together and the answer is simple. In a normal year, banks are the main printer: new spendable money appears mostly because people and firms borrow. In the year to September 2026, bank loans grew by about $1.0 trillion and deposits by about $1.2 trillion. But the government and the Fed together can do the same job, and in some years they do it far more than the banks. That combination is printing money in everything but name.

blocks.caption: Two ways new spendable money is made. The banks run every day. The government and the Fed switch on in emergencies, and then they are bigger.

items: The government spends more than it collects in taxes. When it pays a salary, a pension or a stimulus check, a new deposit lands in someone's bank account. Spending is what actually puts the money in public hands.
To cover the gap, the Treasury sells bonds.

Whether new money is left over depends on who ends up holding those bonds. If households and funds buy them with savings they already had, money only moves around and nothing new is left. If banks buy them, or the Fed buys them in the market from dealers and pension funds, the public keeps the new deposits and the bonds sit with the banks or the Fed. New money remains.

cols: Who ends up holding the new bonds
Is new spendable money left over?
rows: Households and funds, paying with savings they already had
No. Money moves to the government and comes back
Yes. The public has the deposit, the bank has the bond
The Fed, buying from dealers and pension funds in the market
Yes. The Fed has paid for it with new reserves it created

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Think of two printers in an office. The banks' printer runs all day, printing a little each time someone signs a loan, and it shreds the pages again as loans are paid back. The government and the Fed share a second printer kept in a locked room. It needs two keys: Congress must approve the spending, and the Fed must choose to buy the bonds. When both keys turn, as in 2020, it prints faster than anything the banks can do.

The clearest case is 2020 to 2021. Bank deposits jumped $5.45 trillion, about 35%. Most of it came from government spending on stimulus checks, business support loans and unemployment benefits, while the Fed bought about 59% of the new marketable Treasury debt. Bank lending played only a small part that time.
Then why do people say the government cannot just print?

items: The Fed decides, not the Treasury. The law lets the Fed buy only in the open market, for its own reasons such as interest rates or market stability, and it can stop or reverse. Since 2022 it has been shrinking its bond holdings, which pulls money back out.

The bond market votes. If investors think a government is leaning on the printer, they demand higher interest rates. That is part of why the US 10-year yield is near 5% and the interest bill passed $1 trillion a year.
There is friction. Congress must approve the spending, the debt ceiling has to be dealt with, and every auction has to find buyers.

blocks.text: The two kinds of money behave differently over time. Bank-loan money is temporary: when the loan is repaid, the money disappears. Deficit money tends to stay, because the government rarely pays its debt down overall. It rolls the bonds over, so the money it spent remains in circulation. That is why the old worry that governments finance themselves by creating money is basically right, even though some of the old explanations of how it happens are outdated.

blocks.q: In 2020 bank deposits rose by trillions while bank lending barely grew. Which printer was running, and what two things had to happen?
blocks.a: The emergency printer. The government had to spend far more than it taxed, and the Fed and banks had to end up holding much of the new debt. Together that left trillions of new deposits in public hands.

blocks.text: Fifty-five years of money creation: downstairs banks versus the upstairs printer, 1971 to 2026

Since the dollar left gold in 1971, how much new money came from banks lending, and how much from the Fed buying bonds upstairs? The chart below puts the two printers side by side for every year, using the Federal Reserve's own data. The gold bars are the yearly change in commercial bank loans. The blue bars are the yearly change in the bonds the Fed holds (Treasuries plus mortgage bonds). The dots are the actual change in the money supply (M2).

blocks.caption: Yearly change in commercial bank loans (gold) and in the Fed's bond holdings (blue), with the change in M2 (dots), 1971 to 2026. Bars below the line mean that printer was shrinking. 2026 runs to September for loans, 21 October for the Fed and August for M2.

items: 1971 to 2007: the banks did almost all of it. In every decade the Fed's share of the two printers was only 4% to 13%. Its bond buying in those years mostly supplied the paper cash people wanted to hold.
2008 to 2014: the first emergency. Bank loans actually fell by $481 billion in 2009, while the Fed bought bonds worth $3.44T over the period. Upstairs took about 75% of the work.
2015 to 2019: the banks took over again, adding $2.43T of loans while the Fed shrank its holdings by about $449B.
2020 to 2021: the biggest switch-on ever. The Fed bought $4.52T of bonds against $681B of new bank loans, about 87% upstairs. M2 jumped $6.15T in two years, the fastest rise in the record.

2022 to 2025: the printer ran backwards. The Fed shrank its bonds by about $2.00T while banks lent $2.60T. M2 rose only $853B over four years, and fell in 2022 and 2023, the first full-year falls in the official M2 record, which starts in 1959.
2026 so far: both printers are adding again, banks about $784B and the Fed about $201B.

The whole period: banks added about $13.79T of loans and the Fed about $6.43T of bonds. Roughly two thirds downstairs and one third upstairs, but the upstairs third came in two short bursts. M2 grew from about $0.63 trillion at the end of 1970 to about $23.3 trillion in August 2026, roughly 37 times.

blocks.text: How to read the bars fairly. They are the two main engines, not a complete accounting, so they do not add up exactly to the change in M2. Banks also create deposits by buying Treasuries themselves (about $1.9 trillion over the period), the Treasury's cash balance at the Fed swings up and down, and people move money in and out of cash. The blue bar is also the upper limit of upstairs money reaching the public, because Fed buying adds spendable deposits only when the seller is not a bank. Bank loans here are commercial banks only.

blocks.q: Looking at the chart, in which two periods did the upstairs printer do most of the work, and what happened to the money supply right after the second one?
blocks.a: 2008 to 2014 and 2020 to 2021. After 2021 the Fed shrank its bonds by about $2 trillion, and M2 fell in 2022 and 2023 for the first time in the official record.

rules: Ask which floor moved. Reserves are money for banks. Deposits are money for you.
The Fed creates reserves whenever it buys. It creates spendable deposits only when the seller is not a bank.
Auctions and taxes pull money up into the Treasury's account. Spending pushes it back down.
A deficit adds to your money only if banks, the Fed or parked cash fund it.
Banks create money by lending and by buying. Repayments and sales destroy it.
Banks are the everyday printer. The government plus the Fed is the emergency printer.

chapters.title: The musical chairs question
chapters.kicker: If all money is borrowed and interest is owed on top, can everyone ever pay? The honest answer is yes in a quiet world, and not always in a real one.

blocks.text: Chapter 6 showed that money is born as debt. That raises a question almost everyone hits sooner or later, and the owner of this project put it in a sharp form.
Imagine I give a person my own currency YYY$10, but I tell them they must pay me back 5% interest, but no matter how much they work they can't repay if there is only YYY$10 in circulation.
blocks.by: The owner of this project, in their own words

blocks.text: It feels like musical chairs. Ten chairs, ten and a half people. Someone must always be left standing, or someone must always borrow more to keep the music playing. Let us test the intuition carefully, because it is half right, and the half that is right matters a great deal.

blocks.caption: The worry: YYY$10 in circulation, YYY$10.50 owed. If the stock of money is all there is, someone must default or borrow more.

blocks.text: Why it feels impossible
The worry treats money as a fixed pile, a stock. You hand out 10. You ask for 10.50 back. There are only 10 in existence. Arithmetic seems to say no.

The missing piece is time. Money is not used once. It moves. The same coin can pay many debts in a year, because each person who receives it spends it again. Economists call how often money changes hands its velocity. Debts are paid from flows over time, not from the stock all at once.
The real mechanism: the lender spends

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: You are the lender on a small island. You lend YYY$10 to Bea, a fisher, at 5% a year. Each year Bea owes you YYY$0.50 of interest. Where does she get it? From you. You need to eat, so you buy YYY$0.50 of fish from Bea each year. She takes that YYY$0.50 and pays you the interest. Next year, the same thing. The money supply never changes. It stays at YYY$10. Bea pays her interest forever. Nobody is left standing.

Interest is a payment for a service, the use of money over time. As long as the person who receives interest spends it back into the economy, on goods, wages, rent or taxes, the money circulates and can be earned again. Even repaying the principal is possible. Bea can sell you more fish over time and pay down the YYY$10. When she finishes, the money she borrowed is gone, because the loan that created it is gone. That is not a failure. It is the loop from Chapter 6 running in reverse.

Economists who modeled this carefully, including critics of mainstream economics such as Steve Keen, have shown that a pure credit economy can pay interest in a steady state without needing endless new loans. So the strict version of the musical chairs claim, that interest can never be paid without more debt, is not correct.

blocks.myth: Because banks only create the principal and never the interest, the system needs ever more debt just to pay interest, or it collapses.
blocks.reality: Interest is paid out of the circulating flow of money, and banks spend their interest income on salaries, rent, dividends and taxes, which puts it back into circulation. In a steady state, interest can be paid indefinitely. The real dangers come from somewhere else, and they are listed below.

blocks.text: Where the intuition is right
Now the important part. The owner's instinct points at real weaknesses. They are just different from the arithmetic one.

items: Savers who do not spend. If the people receiving interest save it instead of spending it, money piles up with them and drains from everyone else. If savers as a group want their savings to keep growing, someone else must keep going deeper into debt. This is an accounting fact, made famous by the economist Wynne Godley: for every saver accumulating financial assets, some sector, households, businesses, government or foreigners, must be adding debt.

Debt can outgrow income. Paying interest is possible. Paying more and more interest on debts that grow faster than incomes is not sustainable. Global debt is about $365 trillion, roughly 310% of world output, according to the Institute of International Finance in 2026.
Repayment destroys money. If many borrowers try to pay down debt at once, deposits vanish, spending falls, prices and incomes drop, and the remaining debts get harder to pay.
Panics need cash now, not over time. In a crisis everyone wants to settle at once. Then the stock of money really is too small for the pile of claims, unless a central bank steps in.

blocks.text: The more the debtors pay, the more they owe.
blocks.by: Irving Fisher, The Debt-Deflation Theory of Great Depressions, 1933

blocks.text: Fisher saw this in the Great Depression. When everyone sells assets and cuts spending to repay debt, prices fall. Falling prices make each remaining dollar of debt heavier. Paying down debt can make debt burdens worse.
Minsky: stability breeds instability

The economist Hyman Minsky described three kinds of borrowers. Hedge borrowers can pay both interest and principal from income. Speculative borrowers can pay interest from income but must keep rolling over the principal. Ponzi borrowers cannot even pay the interest from income, and must borrow more or sell assets that they hope keep rising.

Minsky's key idea is that long calm periods push people from the first kind toward the third. Good times make lenders and borrowers confident, so they take on more debt against rising asset prices. Then a small shock, like a dip in house prices, reveals that many borrowers were Ponzi borrowers all along. The 2008 crisis is often called a Minsky moment, a phrase coined by economist Paul McCulley.

blocks.caption: The debt treadmill: when debt grows faster than income, the interest bill rises, so more borrowing is needed just to keep pace. Calm years tempt more people onto the faster belt.

blocks.text: Why credit growth became structural after 1971

Under gold, a bank boom eventually ran into a gold shortage and stopped. After 1971 that brake was gone. Each time a slump threatened, central banks could cut rates and governments could borrow, so recessions were shorter but debt rarely got cleared out. Over decades, debt grew faster than incomes. The system became like a bicycle that is stable only while it keeps moving forward.

The US government is the clearest current case. According to Treasury data gathered by this project, the government spent about $7.40 trillion in fiscal year 2026 and collected about $5.40 trillion, a deficit of about $1.99 trillion. Even before interest, it ran a primary deficit of about $941 billion, close to 2.9% of the economy. Interest itself cost about $1.05 trillion. The average rate on its marketable debt is about 3.5%, but new borrowing costs closer to 4.9%, and about 36% of the debt reprices within a year. Unless deficits shrink or rates fall, the interest bill climbs on its own.

The owner's notes say there is only about $15,000 of liquid money per person on earth against about $346 trillion of global debt, and conclude that we live in a world of scarce settlement capacity, not scarce money. The figures need updating: world broad money is now about $19,500 per person, and global debt is about $365 trillion. But the insight is sharp. Normally debts are paid slowly from flows, so a small stock of money services a huge stock of debt. In a panic, everyone wants settlement at once, and the stock is far too small. That is exactly why central banks act as lenders of last resort in a crisis.

blocks.q: In the island story, what single behavior would turn the YYY$10 economy into a real musical chairs game?
blocks.a: If you, the lender, stopped spending your interest and hoarded it. Then money would drain out of circulation into your savings, and Bea would eventually be unable to pay without borrowing more or defaulting.

blocks.q: Is it true that interest can never be paid without new loans?
blocks.a: No. In a steady state, interest can be paid indefinitely as long as interest income is spent back into circulation. The real risks are debt growing faster than income, savers hoarding, mass repayment shrinking the money supply, and panics.

rules: Interest can be paid from a circulating flow. Debt that grows faster than income cannot be paid forever.
When everyone repays at once, money shrinks and debts get heavier. Pace your debt so you never have to sell in a panic.
Calm years breed risky borrowing. Be most careful when lending feels safest.

connects.how: The circulation in this chapter is the loop of Chapter 6 seen over time.
Deleveraging and debt deflation are the dark side of the deflationary seasons.
Debt that outgrows income is a recurring feature of declining empires.
Who gets the new credit decides who can enter the board game.

chapters.title: The seasons of money
chapters.kicker: Money has weather. In some decades it melts, in others it hardens, and the same choice can make you rich in one season and poor in the next.

blocks.text: So far we have looked at how money is made. Now we look at how it behaves over time. Prices do not move in a straight line. They move in long seasons, some inflationary, some deflationary. Most people live through only two or three seasons, so they assume the one they grew up in is normal. The rulebook exists so you do not make that mistake.
Two kinds of weather

items: Inflation: prices in general rise, so each unit of money buys less. Debts get lighter in real terms. Savings in cash shrink in real terms.
Deflation: prices in general fall, so each unit of money buys more. Debts get heavier in real terms. Cash gains real value, but jobs and incomes usually suffer.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Think of money as ice. In a warm season, inflation, ice held in your hand melts, so you want to turn it into something that does not melt, like a house or a tool, and owing ice to someone is cheap because it shrinks while you owe it. In a cold season, deflation, ice keeps its shape and even grows, so holding ice is smart and owing ice is dangerous because your debt grows heavier.
A timeline of seasons, 1870 to 2026

blocks.caption: Seasons of money from 1870 to 2026: inflationary eras (wars, the 1970s, 2021 onward) and deflationary or disinflationary eras (1873 to 1896, 1929 to 1933, 1982 to 2020).

Bank failures, money supply fell about a third
War and postwar inflation with capped rates
War debt, Fed held rates down
Deficits, oil shocks, loose policy, no gold anchor

blocks.text: The last row comes from this project's 2026 data. US consumer energy prices rose about 20.4% over a year, oil traded near $98 a barrel in October, and a key inflation measure ran at 5.0% annualized in the second quarter. Real hourly pay fell about 0.7% in the year to September 2026. The Fed under Kevin Warsh raised rates in September 2026, against the President's wishes.

Financial repression is the polite name for a quiet trick governments use to shrink debt. They keep interest rates below inflation, so lenders to the government lose real value every year. Economists Carmen Reinhart and Belen Sbrancia showed in 2011 that the US and UK used this after the Second World War to cut their debt burdens substantially. A mild version is happening now: the average interest rate on US government debt is about 3.2 to 3.5%, while nominal income has grown about 5.7% a year over the past decade, so inflation is quietly shrinking the debt relative to the economy.
Why governments prefer mild inflation

items: It shrinks debt. A government that owes trillions benefits when each future dollar is worth a little less.
Wages are sticky downward. People resist pay cuts. With mild inflation, a business can let real wages adjust by giving smaller raises instead of cutting pay, which keeps more people employed.
It leaves room to cut rates. If inflation is 2% and rates are 4%, a central bank can cut rates enough to make borrowing cheap in real terms during a slump. With zero inflation, there is less room.
Deflation is scarier. Once people expect falling prices, they delay buying, firms delay hiring, and debts grow heavier. That spiral is hard to stop.

blocks.text: New Zealand adopted the first formal inflation target in 1990. The Federal Reserve formally adopted a 2% target in 2012. The owner calls inflation a circulation incentive, a leaking bucket that pushes people to spend or invest rather than hoard cash. That is a fair description of how a mild target works, and it is also why holding idle cash is a slow loss in most modern seasons.
Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon.

Friedman's line is famous and partly true. Over long periods, sustained high inflation does come with fast money growth. But most economists today add that supply shocks, like the oil embargoes of the 1970s or the 2026 energy shock, can drive prices up for a while even without fast money growth, and that expectations matter a great deal. Where scholars disagree is how much weight to give each.
Deflation traps

The United States from 1929 to 1933 is the classic trap. About 9,000 banks failed. The money supply fell by about a third, as Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz documented. Prices fell by about a quarter. Unemployment reached about 25%. Fisher's debt deflation, from Chapter 9, ran at full speed.

Japan is the modern case. After its stock and property bubble burst around 1990, banks were slow to admit losses, households and firms paid down debt for years, and prices drifted slightly downward for much of the period from the late 1990s to the early 2010s. The Nikkei stock index did not regain its 1989 peak until 2024. The economist Richard Koo called this a balance sheet recession: everyone repaying debt at once, so nobody borrows to spend.
A store of value changes jobs with the season
Here is a subtle point that most people never notice. An asset is not simply safe or risky. It is a tool that works in some seasons and fails in others.

blocks.text: Gold is usually called an inflation hedge, but from 1980 to 2001, a period that still had inflation, gold lost most of its value in real terms. What gold really hedges is a loss of trust in the money or the people managing it. When trust is high and real interest rates are high, gold tends to struggle. When trust falls, gold shines. In 2025 central banks bought about 863 tonnes of gold, a sign that some governments trust the system less.

blocks.myth: There is one safe asset you can buy and forget.
blocks.reality: Safety depends on the season. Long-term US government bonds are free of default risk, but holders lost close to half their market value from 2020 to 2023 as rates rose. Cash is safe from crashes but loses value to inflation. The most reliable protection is to understand which season you are in and to avoid betting everything on one season continuing.

blocks.q: You have a fixed-rate mortgage and inflation jumps to 8%. Are you better or worse off in real terms?
blocks.a: Better off as a borrower, as long as your income keeps up. Your fixed payments and remaining debt shrink in real terms because each dollar you repay buys less.

blocks.q: Why did Japan's long stagnation happen even though interest rates were near zero?
blocks.a: Households, firms and banks were focused on repairing their balance sheets after the 1990 bust, so they paid down debt instead of borrowing to spend. Cheap money did not help when nobody wanted to borrow.

rules: Know your season. Ask whether money is melting or hardening before you decide to save, borrow or invest.
Mild inflation is the default policy goal. Idle cash slowly loses in most modern seasons.
No asset is safe in every season. Spread your bets across seasons, not just across names.

chapters.title: The deflation debate: would anyone spend a money that grows?
chapters.kicker: If a dollar buys more tomorrow, why spend it today? The oldest argument against hard money, why it never ends, and what both sides miss.

blocks.text: Chapter 10 showed that money has seasons. This chapter takes one question from the cold season and follows it all the way down, because it sits under almost every fight about gold, Bitcoin and central banks. The question is simple: if I know my $1 will buy more tomorrow, why would I spend it today?
The case against a growing money

items: Prices are expected to fall, so people wait to buy cars, homes and machines.
Shops and factories sell less, so they cut prices further and cut jobs.
Workers who lose income spend even less. Borrowers find their debts heavier, because the money they owe is worth more while their income shrinks.
Defaults rise, banks pull back, and the loop feeds itself. Economists call this a deflationary spiral. Irving Fisher described its debt side in 1933 and called it debt deflation.

blocks.text: This is why almost every major central bank aims for a little inflation, usually 2%, rather than zero or falling prices. The cases they point to are the Great Depression and Japan's lost decades, both in chapter 10.
The case for a growing money

items: You still need things today. Food, rent, medicine and school fees do not wait. People keep buying phones and televisions even though they know next year's model will be cheaper and better.
Waiting has a cost. A sofa you buy next year is a year without a sofa. Economists call this time preference: people value having things sooner.
History has good deflations. From the 1870s to the 1890s US prices fell for years while output, railways and industry grew fast, because new technology made things cheaper to produce.

The data are weaker than the fear. A 2015 Bank for International Settlements study covering about 140 years and up to 38 economies found only a weak link between falling consumer prices and slower growth, mostly driven by the Great Depression. The damage came mainly from falling property prices combined with private debt.
Discipline. When money cannot be printed, governments and companies must fund projects from real savings, so fewer bad projects get started.

blocks.text: Why the fight never ends: two sides, two different deflations

blocks.caption: The same falling prices with opposite causes. Good deflation starts with cheaper production. Bad deflation starts with collapsing demand and heavy debt.

blocks.text: The argument goes in circles because each side pictures a different deflation. The hard-money side pictures good deflation: things get cheaper because we got better at making them, incomes hold steady, and every paycheck buys more. The central-bank side pictures bad deflation: prices fall because nobody is buying, while debts stay fixed. Both have happened. Which one you get depends mostly on one thing: how much debt is in the system when prices start to fall.

Today's world carries record debt. The US government alone owes $40.44T. In a deflation every one of those dollars gets heavier to repay. That is the real reason no heavily indebted government will choose a deflationary money. The debate sounds like it is about shoppers delaying purchases. Underneath, it is about who carries the debt.
Spend the worse money, keep the better one

An older rule explains what people actually do when they can choose between two monies. It is Gresham's law: bad money drives out good. People spend the money that is losing value and hoard the one that is gaining. In Tudor England people spent the clipped and debased coins and kept the full-weight ones at home.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: On 22 May 2010 a programmer named Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoin for two pizzas, the first well-known purchase of real goods with Bitcoin. At about $86,000 a coin in early October 2026, those coins would be worth roughly $860 million. After stories like that, almost nobody spends Bitcoin on pizza. They spend dollars and keep the Bitcoin. That is Gresham's law in a single slice.

So a money expected to grow tends to become a store of value, while a money that slowly melts becomes the one people spend. That is why the medium of exchange argument against deflationary money is partly right and partly beside the point. People do not stop spending. They spend the other money. Today that other money is the dollar, or a dollar stablecoin, sitting next to gold or Bitcoin in the same wallet.

blocks.myth: Falling prices always mean a weak economy.
blocks.reality: Prices of televisions, computers and phones have fallen for decades while the industries making them boomed. What hurts is falling prices plus heavy debt plus collapsing demand, not falling prices alone.

blocks.text: This matters for the future this desk studies. Robots, AI and cheap solar push the cost of making things down, a good-deflation force. A debt-heavy system cannot let that show up as falling prices, so it creates enough new money to keep prices rising gently. The productivity gain does not vanish. It flows to whoever receives the new money first and to owners of scarce things such as land, energy and platforms. That is the link to the Cantillon effect and the platform toll booths in chapter 18.

blocks.q: If prices are expected to fall 2% a year, why might a family still buy a fridge today?
blocks.a: Because it needs a fridge now. Waiting a year to save 2% means a year without a fridge. Real needs and time preference keep spending going. A spiral starts when incomes fall and debts bite, not from cheaper prices alone.

blocks.q: Why do most people spend dollars and keep gold or Bitcoin?
blocks.a: Gresham's law. When two monies circulate side by side, people spend the one expected to lose value and hoard the one expected to gain.

rules: A deflation is good or bad depending on its cause and on how much debt sits in the system.
People do not stop spending when one money grows. They spend the other money and keep the growing one.
The fight over inflation is a fight over who carries the debt.

chapters.title: Why empires and their currencies fall
chapters.kicker: No money has ruled forever. The ones that fell usually fell the same way: war, debt and a slow watering down of the promise.

blocks.text: The dollar has been the world's main money for about a century. Before it, other currencies held that role and lost it. This chapter walks through the most famous cases, looks for the common pattern, and then asks honestly what is different today. It is the chapter where humility matters most, because history rhymes but never repeats exactly.
Rome: the long watering down

Chapter 2 told the story of the denarius. Rome's army and borders were enormously expensive. As conquest slowed, new silver stopped arriving, but the bills kept coming. Emperors filled the gap by debasing the coin. By the late 200s AD the coinage had collapsed, prices had soared and the state increasingly collected taxes in goods rather than in its own worthless coins.

The story has a twist that few people know. The emperor Constantine introduced a gold coin, the solidus, in the early 300s. In the eastern half of the empire, which became Byzantium, the solidus kept its gold content for roughly 700 years, until it was debased in the 1000s. It was the dollar of the medieval Mediterranean. A money can stay honest for centuries when the state that issues it chooses to keep it so.
Spain: rich in silver, poor in the end

In 1545 Spanish colonizers found a mountain of silver at Potosi, in today's Bolivia. Silver from Potosi and Mexico flooded into Spain for over a century, and the Spanish silver coin, the piece of eight, became a world money used from China to the American colonies.

Yet the Spanish crown went bankrupt again and again. Philip II stopped payments to his bankers in 1557, 1560, 1575 and 1596. The silver was spent on wars across Europe and on imports, and it flowed out as fast as it came in. Prices across Europe rose several-fold over the 1500s, an episode called the price revolution. Historians still debate how much of that inflation came from American silver and how much from population growth. What is clear is that easy money without a productive base did not make Spain lastingly strong.
The Dutch: the first modern financial center

In the 1600s the small Dutch Republic became the trading and financial center of Europe. Amsterdam created the Dutch East India Company in 1602, one of the first companies with tradable shares, and the Bank of Amsterdam in 1609, whose bank money was trusted across Europe. Dutch guilders and bills of exchange financed world trade.

Decline came through a mix of costly wars with England and France, rising debt, and loss of trading edge as Britain grew. A disastrous war with Britain from 1780 to 1784 hit hard. It later emerged that the Bank of Amsterdam had secretly lent heavily to the struggling East India Company and the city, which undermined trust in its money. The company was dissolved in 1799 and the bank was wound down in 1819.
Britain: the pound sterling

Britain built the most successful money of the 1800s. The Bank of England, founded in 1694, and the gold standard of Chapter 2 made sterling the currency of world trade and London the world's banker. Britain carried enormous debt after the Napoleonic Wars, more than twice its economy, but the Industrial Revolution grew the economy fast enough to carry it. High debt alone did not sink Britain.

Two world wars did. Britain sold overseas investments and borrowed heavily from the United States to fight. After 1945 it was a large debtor with a weakened industry. The decline of sterling then took decades: a convertibility crisis in 1947, American financial pressure during the Suez crisis of 1956, a devaluation in 1967, and a loan from the IMF in 1976. The economist Barry Eichengreen showed that the dollar actually overtook sterling as a reserve currency as early as the mid-1920s, fell back in the 1930s, and only pulled clearly ahead after the Second World War. Changes at the top are slow and messy, not sudden.
The common pattern

blocks.caption: A common pattern in past declines: rising power and trust, a peak with a trusted currency and financial center, then war costs, rising debt, debasement or inflation, and a rival taking the lead. A framework, not a law.

items: A rising power wins trust through productive strength, trade and sound money.
Its currency becomes the world's preferred money, and its capital becomes the financial center. Borrowing becomes cheap.
Cheap borrowing funds wars, overseas commitments and consumption. Debt rises faster than the productive base.
To pay the bills, the state debases its coin or inflates its paper, and trust starts to fade.
A rival with stronger production offers an alternative. The center of money moves, usually after a great war.

blocks.text: A popular chart, often shown by investment firms, lists the leading currencies of the last 600 years with lifespans of roughly 80 to 110 years each: Portugal, Spain, the Netherlands, France, Britain and the United States. Treat it with care. Historians argue about whether reserve currency even means much before the 1800s, the dates are rough, and as the sterling story shows, top currencies often share the stage for decades. The chart is a conversation starter, not a countdown clock.
Dalio's big cycle: one framework

The investor Ray Dalio, in his 2021 book Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order, describes a big cycle of empires. He tracks measures such as education, innovation, competitiveness, economic output, share of world trade, military strength, financial center strength and reserve currency status. In his account, empires rise as education and innovation improve, peak when their currency and financial center dominate, and decline as debts mount, money is printed, wealth gaps widen, internal conflict grows and a rival rises.

The framework is useful because it makes you look at many measures at once. It is not a law of nature. Critics point out that the sample of empires is small, that the stages are easier to see in hindsight than in real time, and that very different histories get squeezed into one shape. Use it as a checklist for questions, not a calendar for predictions.
If something cannot go on forever, it will stop.
blocks.by: Herbert Stein, economist and adviser to Presidents Nixon and Ford, 1980s

blocks.text: What looks familiar now

items: Interest now costs more than defense. In fiscal year 2026 the US paid about $1,052 billion in net interest against about $965 billion for national defense, the third year in a row. The historian Niall Ferguson has argued that a great power spending more on debt service than on defense is a warning sign.
Debt rising faster than the economy. US debt held by the public is about 100% of GDP, and the deficit was about $1.99 trillion in 2026.
Allies hedging. Foreign official holdings of Treasuries at the New York Fed fell about $254 billion from February to October 2026, and central banks bought about 863 tonnes of gold in 2025.
A tax base leaning on wages. About 86% of federal receipts in 2026 came from individual income and payroll taxes, while machines and capital are taking a larger share of income.

blocks.text: What is genuinely different

items: No ready successor. The euro has no single government bond market and no single treasury behind it. China keeps controls on money leaving the country, which limits the yuan as a reserve. This project's research found that rivals' strongest cards today are in hardware, like rare earth magnets, batteries and solar technology, not in currency.

US debt is in its own currency. Spain owed its bankers in silver it could not create. The US owes dollars it can create. It is unlikely to default outright. The risk is inflation and higher interest rates, which is a slower, quieter kind of decline.
Digital rails may extend the dollar's reach. Most of the growth in dollar stablecoins went to holders outside the US, spreading dollar use rather than shrinking it.
Network effects are global and instant. Payments, oil, loans and contracts all run on dollar plumbing, and switching costs are enormous.

rows: S1: the dollar system extends, absorbing new rails
S2: a neutral layer (for example gold or a neutral token) gains a real role
S3: energy or compute becomes a monetary anchor

blocks.text: These are this project's own judgment, made in October 2026, not facts. Notice two things. The dollar stays the most likely single outcome for years. But the chance of something messier grows the further out you look. Both of those can be true at once.

blocks.q: What do Rome, Spain and Britain have in common in the decline of their money?
blocks.a: Each faced war costs and debts larger than their productive base could carry, leaned on debasement, borrowing or inflation to pay, and saw trust and leadership shift to a stronger rival.

blocks.q: Why is Dalio's big cycle a framework rather than a law?
blocks.a: It is based on a small number of historical cases, its stages are clearer in hindsight than in real time, and very different histories are fitted to one shape. It is useful for asking questions, not for predicting dates.

rules: Watch the ratio of interest to defense, and of debt to output. Those ratios have warned before.
Money centers move slowly and messily. Do not bet on a sudden collapse or on permanence.
A strong money needs a strong productive base. Easy money without production has never lasted.

connects.how: Rome's debasement and the gold standard's discipline are two ends of the same story.
The pillars of the dollar loop are what make this empire's currency different.
Debt outgrowing income, from the musical chairs chapter, is the engine of decline.
The rivals and new rails on today's board are the live test of this chapter.

chapters.title: The country leaderboard: deep markets and the game nations play
chapters.kicker: Why surplus nations park their savings in America, why climbing the leaderboard is so hard, and what it really took for each number one to get there and to fall.

blocks.text: Imagine every country on a leaderboard ranked by how much the world trusts its money. Near the top is a strange fact: some of the hardest working, highest saving nations on earth send a large share of their savings to the United States, a country that saves little and borrows a lot. To understand why, you need three ideas: deep markets, governance incentives and game theory.
What makes a market deep

A deep market is one where you can put in or take out enormous sums, quickly, at a fair price, and trust that the rules will not change on you. Few markets qualify. The US Treasury market is the deepest. Its qualities read like a checklist.

blocks.caption: The qualities that make savers worldwide choose one market over their own.

items: Size: tens of trillions of dollars of bonds, so even a central bank can buy or sell billions without moving the price much.
Liquidity: buyers and sellers are always there, every hour, through dealers, futures and repo.
Rule of law: independent courts, contracts that hold, and property that is not taken on a whim.
Open doors: money can leave whenever the owner wants. No exit queue, no permission slip.
A trusted central bank and a currency others already use for trade, debt and oil.
Hedging tools: futures, swaps and options let holders protect themselves.
Security: the military and alliances that protect trade routes and the system itself.

blocks.text: Notice the trade-off hidden in that list. The US gives up some control (it lets money in and out freely and lets courts bind the government) and in return earns the world's trust. Countries that want to keep tight control of their money cannot offer the same deal. That single trade-off explains much of the leaderboard.
Why surplus countries send their savings to America

When an exporter in Japan, China, Korea, Taiwan or the Gulf sells to the world, it earns dollars. If all those dollars were converted into local currency, the local currency would rise, exports would get dearer and factories would lose orders. So, often through the central bank, the dollars are kept as dollars and parked in the safest dollar asset available: Treasuries.

items: Stay competitive: holding the dollars instead of selling them keeps the home currency cheap and exports flowing.
Buy insurance: after the 1997 Asian crisis, countries that ran short of dollars were forced into painful IMF programs. Many vowed never again and built large dollar reserves.
No deep home alternative: many local bond markets are too small, too controlled or too easy to freeze to hold trillions.
Protect the wealthy: elites in less secure systems prefer assets where courts protect property, so private money follows the official money abroad.
Oil and commodities: these are priced in dollars, so exporters earn dollars and often recycle them through sovereign wealth funds.

blocks.text: How that trickles down into the home economy

Parking savings abroad is a governance choice, and ordinary citizens pay part of the bill. A deliberately cheap currency makes imports, fuel and foreign goods dearer for households. Savings that could have financed homes, wages or local businesses instead finance American borrowing. Exporters and the state gain, households consume less than they produce. On the other side, Americans enjoy cheap imports and cheap credit while factory towns hollow out, as chapter 4 showed. Each side's elite chose the arrangement, and each side's workers live with its costs.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Two neighbors. One works long hours, sells most of what it makes to the other, and lends the payment back so the other can keep buying. The lender's family lives modestly. The borrower's family lives well but its workshop goes quiet. Neither can easily stop: if the lender stops lending, its buyer disappears. If the borrower stops buying, the lender's factory stalls. That is the quiet bargain behind the dollar.

Economist Larry Summers called this mutual dependence a 'balance of financial terror' in 2004. Each side holds the other hostage, which is why sudden moves are rare and why the game is played with signals, slow shifts and patience.
The game theory of the leaderboard

blocks.caption: A currency war as a prisoner's dilemma. Each country is tempted to cheat, and if both do, both lose.

items: A coordination game: everyone uses the dollar because everyone else does. Switching only pays if many switch together, and the first to switch pays the most. That is why the leader keeps its place long after its advantages fade.

A prisoner's dilemma: each country gains by weakening its currency or adding tariffs, but if all do it, trade shrinks and all lose. The 1930s round of competitive devaluations and tariffs is the classic case.
A repeated game: nations meet again and again, so reputation matters. A country that keeps its promises can borrow cheaply for centuries. One that breaks them pays for decades.

A war of exhaustion: rivals drain each other through arms races, sanctions and tariff wars. History suggests leaders more often fall from overstretch and debt than from being overtaken in a single contest. Historian Paul Kennedy called this imperial overstretch.

The elite trap: a country rises on cheap labor and heavy investment, but climbing higher requires giving up control: floating the currency, opening the capital account, independent courts. The elites who profit from control often block those steps. Economists Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson describe this as extractive institutions resisting inclusive ones. It is one reason so many countries stall in the middle of the leaderboard.

blocks.myth: The country with the biggest economy automatically gets the top currency.
blocks.reality: Currency leadership lags economic leadership by decades. The US economy passed Britain's in the 1870s, yet sterling remained a leading reserve currency into the 1940s and beyond. Trust, habit and deep markets take generations to move.

blocks.text: Notice the pattern. Defaults and devaluations rarely end an empire in one blow. They are symptoms of a deeper strain: spending on war and status that the productive economy can no longer carry. France shows how fast it can turn political: a partial default in 1770 and a debt crisis in the 1780s led to the calling of the Estates General in 1789 and the Revolution.
What it really takes to be number one

items: Produce: a real economy that makes things the world wants.
Protect: security for trade routes and allies.
Promise: institutions that make debt credible, so the state can borrow cheaply in a crisis. Britain after 1688 and Hamilton's America after 1790 both won wars partly because lenders trusted them.
Plumbing: deep, open financial markets that others can use.
People: a culture of work, saving, invention and trust in contracts.
Place: geography that protects and connects, from Britain's channel to America's two oceans.

blocks.text: No single leader had all six forever. Each rose when its mix fit the technology and trade of its age, and each faded when debt, war and complacency ate the mix away. The open question for this century is whether the United States can keep its plumbing and promise strong enough to outlast the strain on the other pillars, and whether any rival is willing to give up enough control to offer a deeper market.
Geography deals the cards, and the deck keeps changing

Place is one of the six pillars, but what makes a place valuable changes with technology. Every era has its own rare and needed thing, and the countries sitting on it get a turn near the top. Then the technology moves, and yesterday's treasure can lose its value almost overnight.

blocks.caption: What the world found rare and needed, era by era. The places that held it rose. Some lost it when technology changed.

blocks.text: Chile's nitrate mines made it rich in the late 1800s, because nitrate was needed for fertilizer and explosives. In 1913 German chemists began making nitrogen in factories, and the boom ended. Botswana grew faster than almost any country from 1965 to 1995 on diamonds, and is now strained because laboratory-grown stones have pushed natural diamond prices down. Today the rare and needed things are battery metals, rare earths, chips, cheap power and compute.
Rich ground, poor people: the resource curse

Having the cards is not the same as winning the hand. South Africa mines about 70% of the world's platinum, 46% of its chromium and 40% of its manganese, according to the US Geological Survey, and holds most of the world's platinum-group reserves. Yet its official unemployment rate was 33.6% in the second quarter of 2026, and 47.4% for people aged 15 to 34. The Democratic Republic of the Congo mines about 72% of the world's cobalt, the metal in most rechargeable batteries, yet remains one of the poorest countries on earth and has suffered decades of war.

blocks.caption: Who captures the value of a mineral. The miner keeps the smallest share. China refines about 79% of the world's cobalt.

blocks.text: Economists call this the resource curse. Its parts fit together. Easy money from the ground lets rulers govern without taxing or serving citizens. Armed groups fight to control the mines. A flood of export dollars lifts the currency and makes every other industry uncompetitive, which is called Dutch disease after the Netherlands' gas boom of the 1960s. And the money is made at the next steps, refining, manufacturing and finance, which happen elsewhere.

blocks.myth: Resource-rich countries stay poor because of their culture or because people are out of touch with modern money habits.
blocks.reality: Habits such as saving in banks, paying tax and trusting contracts do matter, but research points mainly to institutions, and habits follow institutions. People save and invest where titles are safe and money holds its value. Colonial economies were built to dig and ship raw materials out. In South Africa, apartheid barred most people from owning land, skilled jobs and good schools until 1994, and since then power cuts, failing rail and ports, and corruption exposed by the state capture inquiry have held growth back. Change the institutions and the habits change with them.

blocks.text: The exceptions prove the rule. Norway built strong institutions before it found oil, then saved the oil money abroad in a fund that now owns about 1.5% of every listed company in the world. Botswana negotiated a partnership with the diamond company De Beers and spent the money on schools, health and roads. Geography deals the cards. Institutions decide whether a country can play them.

Watch who refines, not just who digs. Indonesia banned exports of raw nickel ore in 2020 to force refining at home, and China's grip on refining battery metals and rare earths gives it more leverage than any mine does. On the country leaderboard, the processing step and the financial step are where rare things turn into power.

blocks.q: Why might a country with huge savings choose to lend them to the US instead of spending them at home?
blocks.a: To keep its own currency cheap for exporters, to hold insurance against a dollar shortage, because its home markets are too small or controlled to hold the savings, and because its elites trust US courts with their wealth. Its households pay part of the cost through dearer imports and lower consumption.

blocks.q: South Africa mines about 70% of the world's platinum. Why has that not made most South Africans rich?
blocks.a: Because the value is captured mostly at later steps and by owners, while the institutions that turn resource money into broad jobs, skills and ownership were weakened by history and poor governance. Rare ground pays only when institutions let it.

rules: Money flows to the deepest, safest, most open market, not the richest country.
A cheap currency helps exporters and taxes households. Ask who inside a country pays for its surplus.
Currency leadership lags economic leadership by decades, so do not expect sudden switches.
Empires rarely fall from one default. They fall when war and debt outgrow the productive base.
Geography deals the cards. Institutions decide whether a country can play them.
Watch who refines and who finances, not just who digs.
