chapters.title: Crypto: Set 2 money, dissected
chapters.kicker: Bitcoin, stablecoins and twenty million other tokens, sorted into three families, tested against the jobs of money, and taken apart with six questions you can use on any coin you ever hear about.

blocks.label: In 60 seconds
items: Chapter 1 said money is a trusted record of who can claim what. Crypto is a new way to keep that record: a shared ledger that no single bank or government runs.

There are three very different families. Bitcoin is a scarce asset that is nobody's debt. Stablecoins are digital dollars backed by Treasury bills. Everything else is closer to a share in a platform, a loyalty point or a lottery ticket.
Lumping them together as 'crypto' is the most common mistake. Each family answers the money questions differently.
So far Set 2 is not replacing Set 1. Stablecoins carry dollars onto new rails, and Bitcoin competes with gold as a neutral store. Set 1 is absorbing Set 2.
To judge any token, ask six questions: who issues it, whose debt is it, what anchors it, which job of money does it do, who can freeze it, and where does its return come from.

items.d: A record of who owns what. Every money in history has been one.
A ledger copied across thousands of computers, updated in blocks and very hard to change afterward.
A unit recorded on a blockchain. It can stand for a coin, a dollar, a share or a vote.
The secret password that moves your tokens. Lose it and nobody can restore it.
A token built to stay worth $1, usually backed by dollars and Treasury bills.

blocks.text: Why crypto matters for what money is

Go back to chapter 1. Money is not the paper or the metal. It is a trusted record of who can claim what, and the fight has always been over who keeps the record: the temple, the king, the goldsmith, the central bank, the commercial bank. Crypto's real invention, published in 2008, is a record kept by a network instead of a keeper. The rules are written in code, anyone can check the ledger, and no single party can quietly edit it.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: On 3 January 2009 the first Bitcoin block was created with a newspaper headline written into it: 'Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks', from The Times of London. Whoever built it was making a point in the middle of the financial crisis: here is a money whose ledger no bank can lose and no government can inflate. The creator, known only as Satoshi Nakamoto, has never been identified.

That is why crypto belongs in this book. It is the first serious attempt since gold to create money that is nobody's debt and nobody's ledger. Chapter 21 showed that almost all modern money is someone's IOU. Bitcoin is the deliberate exception. Whether or not it succeeds, it forces every government to answer an old question in a new form: who should keep the record?
Set 1 and Set 2

This project splits the money world into two sets. Set 1 is the old anchors: gold, government bonds and bank credit. Set 2 is the new rails: blockchains, stablecoins and tokens. After three research rounds the desk's finding is that Set 1 is absorbing Set 2, an acquisition rather than a merger. Stablecoins must hold Treasury bills by law, Wall Street sells Bitcoin through exchange-traded funds approved in January 2024, and asset managers are moving Treasury funds onto blockchains.

blocks.caption: Each new rail ends up tied back to an old anchor.

blocks.text: The three families

blocks.caption: Three families that share a technology and little else. Sizes from mid-October 2026.

blocks.text: Family 1: Bitcoin, digital gold

items: Fixed supply: the code caps it at 21 million coins. About 20.08 million had been mined by August 2026, and an estimated 10% to 20% of those are lost forever with forgotten keys.
Slowing issuance: new coins are created as a reward for running the network, and the reward halves about every four years. The last halving, in April 2024, cut it to 3.125 coins per block.
Nobody's debt: there is no issuer to redeem it and no one who owes you anything. On chapter 21's mirror it sits beside gold.
Size: about $80,900 a coin and about $1.63 trillion in total on 15 October 2026, roughly 60% of all crypto by value.
Wild swings: it fell about 77% from its November 2021 peak to November 2022, and has had several falls of that size.

Governments are circling: a March 2025 executive order created a US Strategic Bitcoin Reserve from coins already seized in court cases. The Treasury Secretary said in August 2025 the US would not buy more.

blocks.text: Test it against the three jobs of money. As a store of value it is a real candidate, scarce and owed by no one, but its swings are far too large for most people's savings. As a medium of exchange it is rarely used, because, as chapter 11 showed with the 10,000-bitcoin pizza, people spend the money that melts and keep the one they expect to grow. As a unit of account it barely exists: almost nothing is priced in Bitcoin. Its realistic job is a neutral store of value next to gold.
Family 2: Stablecoins, dollars on new rails

A stablecoin is a token that tries to stay worth exactly $1. A company holds dollars and short-term Treasury bills, issues a token for each dollar deposited and destroys it when the dollar is taken back out. In October 2026 stablecoins totaled about $303.8 billion, led by Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC. Under the GENIUS Act, signed in July 2025 and taking full effect on 18 January 2027, compliant issuers must hold reserves in cash and Treasury bills of 93 days or less, and may not pay holders interest. The issuer keeps the interest on the bills.

Stablecoins are Set 1 wearing Set 2 clothes. They carry the dollar to anyone with a phone, including savers in weak-currency countries like those in chapter 14, and every new stablecoin dollar is a new buyer of US Treasury bills. Stablecoins already hold about 4.27% of all T-bills. That is why Washington legalized private stablecoins while a January 2025 executive order blocked work on a Federal Reserve digital dollar for the public. A stablecoin is a dollar IOU, so on chapter 21's mirror it sits on the debt side.

Stable does not mean safe. In March 2023 USDC briefly fell to about 87 cents when $3.3 billion of its reserves were stuck at the failing Silicon Valley Bank. In May 2022 TerraUSD, a so-called algorithmic stablecoin backed mainly by its own sister token instead of dollars, collapsed from about $40 billion to almost nothing within days.
Family 3: everything else

More than 20 million tokens had been created by 2025, most through do-it-yourself launch sites, and CoinGecko counts more than half of the ones it tracks as already dead. The survivors follow a handful of business models.

rows: Fuel to run apps on a blockchain, such as Ether (about $288B in October 2026)
Collect fees from everyone who uses the network
A share in a toll road
Loyalty points, or shares without shareholder rights
Votes over how a protocol is run
Bonds, funds or property recorded on a blockchain, such as BlackRock's BUIDL
The same asset with a new ledger

blocks.text: Tokenized US Treasury funds grew about fiftyfold from early 2024 to about $16 billion by August 2026, which is the clearest sign of Set 1 moving onto Set 2 rails. Most of the rest are not money at all in the sense of chapter 1. They are claims on a business, a network or a hope.

blocks.label: Not crypto, but a cousin
blocks.text: A central bank digital currency uses some of the same technology for the opposite purpose: the state keeps the ledger and can see every payment. China's e-CNY is the largest. Since January 2026 its wallet balances count as deposits at commercial banks and can earn interest. Bitcoin was built to take the ledger away from the state. A central bank digital currency brings it closer.
How to dissect any token: six questions

blocks.caption: Six questions that work on any coin, old or new. The last one catches most scams.

items: Who issues it, and can they make more? Find the supply rule and who is able to change it.
Whose debt is it? If someone must redeem it, it is an IOU and you are trusting them. If no one owes it, its value rests only on demand.
What anchors its value? Reserves, scarcity, fees from a working network, or nothing but attention.
Which job of money does it do: spend, store or measure? Or is it really a share, a coupon or a lottery ticket?
Who runs the ledger, and who can freeze or change it? An issuer that can freeze your coins is a bank in all but name.
Where does the return come from? If it pays a yield, someone must be paying it. If you cannot name who, the yield may be paid with newer investors' money.

blocks.caption: Try it. Pick a token and read its dissection. Compare Bitcoin with a stablecoin, then with a meme coin.

blocks.text: Question six would have saved a lot of people in 2022. Terra's Anchor platform paid about 20% a year on its stablecoin when most dollar savings paid under 2%, and at its peak held about $14 billion. The return was topped up from reserves rather than earned, so when the reserves ran low the whole structure collapsed. The same question applied to the FTX exchange, which collapsed in November 2022 after customer deposits were moved to its sister trading firm.
Where crypto sits on the layers of money

blocks.caption: Bitcoin sits beside gold at the narrow, solid bottom because it is nobody's debt. Stablecoins sit on top of Treasuries. Most other tokens belong with the riskiest claims near the top.

blocks.myth: Crypto is backed by nothing, so it is all worthless.
blocks.reality: Some tokens are backed by nothing and are worth nothing. Stablecoins are backed by dollars and bills. Bitcoin is backed by nothing in the way gold is backed by nothing: its value rests on scarcity and demand. Judge each one with the six questions, not by the label.

blocks.myth: Bitcoin will replace the dollar.
blocks.reality: Not as things stand. Almost nothing is priced in Bitcoin, few people spend it, and its swings are too large for wages and rent. Its realistic job is a neutral store of value next to gold. The challenger on the spending side is the stablecoin, and that is the dollar itself.

blocks.text: Why it matters for the future this desk studies

items: It tests who keeps the record. Every government now has to choose between private stablecoins, a state digital currency, or leaving the old bank ledger alone.
It extends the dollar. Stablecoins are becoming one of the largest new sources of demand for US Treasury bills, the captive demand chapter 7 described.

It offers a neutral store. If trust in all government debts weakens, Bitcoin and gold are the two assets that are nobody's IOU. The desk's scenario of a neutral reserve layer stands at about 15% to 2028, 23% from 2028 to 2035 and 28% from 2035 to 2050.
It moves the ledger itself. Tokenized Treasuries and funds could make settlement instant, which changes who earns the float, the fees and the data.

blocks.text: The owner's question: what if the dollar ruler disappears?

blocks.label: The owner's question
blocks.text: Today everything, a share, a company bond, a token, has an easy measuring stick, because the dollar is there. Remove that layer, and we would probably learn to price things in Bitcoin. But right now crypto keeps getting absorbed into Set 1, because most of the world still settles in currencies. If tokens get good enough that nobody needs to convert Solana into stablecoins to buy things, and so many tokens can exist, where does their value come from? It still seems to come from base-layer credit and bond money. And if anyone lucky enough, a lottery winner or someone with a big enough yield, can launch their own token, it looks like a utopia. The opportunity seems enormous, and this is where it stops making sense.

This is chapter 1's question in its newest form: what makes something money, and who decides how everything is measured? It untangles in five pieces, followed by the questions worth carrying with you.
1. The ruler is the hardest job of money

Money has three jobs: spend, store and measure. Crypto has made real progress on the first two. The third, being the ruler everything is priced in, is the hardest, and no token has won it. When you pay with a token through a crypto debit card, the shop's price was set in dollars and your token was sold for dollars at the till. The conversion is invisible, not absent. The European Central Bank finds crypto and stablecoins below 1% of in-store payments in the euro area, in both 2024 and 2026.

blocks.caption: Why the dollar keeps the ruler: every link in an ordinary life is a dollar contract.

blocks.text: The ruler belongs to whatever debts and taxes are written in. Your salary, your rent, your landlord's mortgage, the bank's loans, the government's bonds and your taxes are all dollar contracts. A token can become the ruler only when those debts start being written in it. Chapter 20 showed that taxes give a money its value. El Salvador tested the opposite. It made Bitcoin legal tender in 2021, but its debts, wages and taxes stayed in dollars, use stayed low, and in January 2025, as part of a $1.4 billion IMF deal, it made accepting Bitcoin optional and dropped the state's promise to convert it to dollars.
2. Many monies, one ruler: why markets always rebuild a hub

blocks.caption: Six monies with no common ruler need 15 exchange rates. With one ruler in the middle, each needs only one price.

blocks.text: If every token traded directly against every other, each pair would need its own price. With 10 monies that is 45 exchange rates. With 1,000 it is 499,500. With the more than 20 million tokens created by 2025 it would be about 200 trillion. Nobody can think in that many prices, so markets always choose one hub that everything else is priced through. That is how barter turned into money in chapter 1, and it is happening again inside crypto, where most trading runs through a dollar stablecoin, Ether or Bitcoin acting as the hub.

blocks.caption: Try it. Slide from 2 monies to 20 million and watch how many exchange rates you would need without a common ruler.

blocks.label: This happened before
blocks.text: From 1837 to 1863 America had no national paper currency. Hundreds of banks printed their own notes, and each note traded at its own discount depending on the bank's reputation and how far away it was. Shopkeepers kept bank note reporters, booklets listing what each note was worth and which ones were forgeries. It was a world of many tokens. It ended when Congress taxed state bank notes at 10% in 1865, and their circulation fell from $143 million to $4 million within two years. The ruler went back to one national dollar.

The economist Friedrich Hayek argued in 1976, in The Denationalisation of Money, that private monies should compete and the public would choose the most stable one. Crypto is the first large-scale test of his idea. So far the public keeps choosing the most stable token on offer, and that token is a dollar.
3. Where a token's value really comes from

Your instinct is half right. Today almost every token's price is a dollar price, and most of the money that buys tokens was born as dollar credit, so crypto prices tend to rise when dollar credit is easy and fall when it tightens. But the deeper source of any money's value is the base layer from chapter 21: the real goods, work and assets people will hand over for it. A token is worth what someone will give up to hold it. If everyone held tokens and nobody produced anything, every token would buy nothing.

Bitcoin is scarce, but crypto is not. One coin can be capped at 21 million while anyone can launch a new one in minutes, and more than 20 million have been launched. Each new token is a new claim competing for the same real goods, the same attention and the same buyers' dollars. That is chapter 21's picture again: the claims multiply, and the base layer does not.
4. The lottery winner who launches a token

blocks.caption: The life of a typical launch. Bars show the price. The dashed arrow is where the dollars go.

blocks.text: Launching a token is printing money, and the profit has an old name: seigniorage, from chapter 18. A token costs almost nothing to create. When its founders sell part of it for dollars, they turn newly printed units into real buying power, exactly as a government does when it issues money. That buying power comes from the buyers. Unless the token's network produces something people pay for, the founders' gain is the later buyers' loss. That is why the utopia feels so big: the power to issue money has been opened to everyone, but the pool of real goods all those monies can buy has not grown with it.

rows: Runs a network people pay to use
Users pay fees for a real service, such as settlement or storage
Moves a real asset onto a faster ledger
Cheaper, quicker settlement saves real costs
Launches a token and sells it to later buyers
Seigniorage moves dollars from late buyers to early ones
Pays a high yield from new deposits
Returns come from newer money, as at Terra in 2022

blocks.text: 5. So where is the real opportunity?

items: New rails: cheaper, faster payments across borders, especially for people in weak-currency countries, mostly using dollar stablecoins.
Settlement: tokenized Treasuries and funds that settle in seconds, cutting into the float and fees banks earn today.
Money for machines: AI agents paying each other per request, which this project found already happens mostly in dollar tokens.
Early title to new networks: owning part of a network people truly pay to use, before it is titled. Chapter 21's rule applies: look for the next base layer before it is titled.

The ruler itself: if trust in all government debt ever broke, the next ruler would be whatever is hardest and most widely accepted. Gold did that job for thousands of years, Bitcoin is a candidate, and this project's founding question asks whether energy could be one. The desk puts an energy or compute standard at about 1% to 2028, 3% from 2028 to 2035 and 10% from 2035 to 2050.

blocks.text: The opportunity is real but narrower than it looks. Most of the lasting value is in building rails and owning networks that produce something. Much of the rest is seigniorage passing from late buyers to early ones.
Questions worth carrying with you

blocks.q: If your salary were paid in Solana, what would you pay your rent in, and what is your landlord's mortgage written in?
blocks.a: Dollars, and dollars. Every link in the chain is a dollar contract, so the token is converted somewhere even when you never see it. The ruler changes only when the debts change.

blocks.q: If Bitcoin became the ruler, what would happen to everyone with a mortgage?
blocks.a: If Bitcoin kept rising against goods, prices in Bitcoin would fall and debts written in Bitcoin would get heavier every year. Chapter 11's deflation debate applies: borrowers lose, savers win, and with no central bank there is no lender of last resort in a crisis.

blocks.q: Who would set interest rates in a world of a thousand tokens?
blocks.a: No one centrally. Each token's lenders and borrowers would set their own, and the most trusted token's rate would become the benchmark, the way the Treasury yield is today. The hub returns.

blocks.q: When AI agents pay each other, which ruler will they use?
blocks.a: So far the dollar, through stablecoins. Machines need stable prices even more than people do, because they price millions of tiny transactions. A machine economy is more likely to strengthen the dollar ruler than replace it, unless energy or compute itself becomes the unit.

blocks.q: If anyone can launch a token, what stops the world from drowning in money?
blocks.a: Nothing stops the launching. What stops the drowning is that buyers ignore most tokens, which is why more than half are already dead. Free issuance makes money cheap to create and trust expensive to earn.

blocks.text: General education, not advice. Crypto adds risks that bank money does not have: lost keys with no reset button, hacks, scams that target newcomers, exchanges that fail with customers' money inside, and rules that can change by executive order. Anyone who holds it should know which of the three families they own, and the answer to all six questions.

blocks.q: Is a dollar stablecoin closer to Bitcoin or to a bank deposit?
blocks.a: To a bank deposit. It is an IOU from an issuer, backed by dollars and Treasury bills, worth a dollar only as long as the issuer can redeem it. Bitcoin is nobody's IOU.

blocks.q: A new token promises 30% a year, paid in the token itself. Which of the six questions matters most?
blocks.a: Question six: where does the return come from? If the yield is paid in newly created tokens or from newer investors' money, the high number is a warning, not a feature.

blocks.q: Why do people spend dollars and stablecoins but hold Bitcoin?
blocks.a: Gresham's law from chapter 11: people spend the money they expect to lose value and keep the one they expect to gain.

rules: Crypto is three families, not one. Know which one you are looking at.
Ask whose debt it is. Bitcoin is nobody's IOU. A stablecoin is someone's IOU.
If you cannot say where a yield comes from, the yield is the product being sold.
Set 2 rails keep ending up tied to Set 1 anchors.
The ruler belongs to whatever debts and taxes are written in.
Bitcoin is scarce. Crypto is not.
Launching a token is printing money. Ask who pays for it.

chapters.title: The Rulebook
chapters.kicker: What each generation learned the hard way, written down so the next one does not have to.

blocks.text: Families pass down recipes, tools and stories. They rarely pass down money lessons, because money talk feels private or shameful, and because each generation's crisis feels unique while it is happening. So each generation relearns the same lessons at full price. This chapter is the remedy: a short rulebook, and a list of the mistakes behind it.
Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.
blocks.by: George Santayana, The Life of Reason, 1905

blocks.text: How to use the rulebook

items: Read the rules once straight through. Most will now feel obvious, because the chapters built them.
Pick three rules that you are breaking today. Write them where you will see them.
Before any big money decision, such as a loan, a house, a business or an investment, scan the list and ask which rules apply.
Read the mistakes list with someone younger than you. Ask which mistake they think their own generation is making now.
Add your own rule when life teaches you one. A rulebook that stops growing stops being useful.

blocks.text: The shape of the rules

rows: Your understanding: see the promise behind the paper
Your savings: know what melts and what hardens
Your freedom: never become a forced seller
Your judgment: see who sets the rules and who earns the tolls
Your future: turn income into ownership

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Think of the rulebook as a ship's logbook kept across generations. Each captain wrote down the storms they met, the rocks they hit and the stars that guided them home. The next captain cannot avoid every storm. But a captain who has read the log will recognize the sky before the storm arrives.

The full rulebook and the generational mistakes follow this chapter. They are written to be copied, shared and argued with. They are general education about how money works, not financial advice for any particular person. Where a rule touches your own situation, test it against your own numbers, and against a second opinion.

blocks.q: Which rule from the whole guide would have saved the most people in 2008?
blocks.a: Several apply, but the strongest is: borrow only what you can service through a bad season without selling. Many households and banks were forced sellers when house prices fell.

blocks.q: Why does each generation repeat money mistakes?
blocks.a: Because the last crisis fades from memory, calm years breed confidence, and each new boom tells a story about why this time is different. Writing lessons down and passing them on is the cheapest defense.

rules: Write your lessons down and pass them on. Memory fades, logs do not.
Each generation's crisis wears a new costume. Look for the old pattern underneath.

connects.how: The first rule, that money is a promise, comes from Chapter 1.
The debt rules are the answer to the musical chairs question.
The ownership rules are the answer to the board game question.

rulebook.rule: Money is a promise kept in a ledger. Ask who made the promise and who keeps the ledger.
rulebook.why: The form of money keeps changing, from clay to coins to code. The promise behind it is the thing that holds or fails.

rulebook.rule: Check all three jobs: medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account.
rulebook.why: Few things do all three well. Use each money for the job it is good at.

rulebook.rule: Every deposit is somebody's loan, and every bank loan creates a deposit.
rulebook.why: Modern money is mostly bank credit, so the health of money depends on the health of lending.

rulebook.rule: Interest can be paid from money that circulates. Debt that grows faster than income cannot be paid forever.
rulebook.why: The musical chairs problem appears when savers hoard and debts outgrow incomes, not because interest is unpayable.

rulebook.rule: Borrow only what you can service through a bad season without selling.
rulebook.why: Forced sellers sell at the bottom. Leverage turns a temporary fall into a permanent loss.

rulebook.rule: Know your season. Ask whether money is melting or hardening.
rulebook.why: The same choice, like holding cash or long bonds, wins in one season and loses in the next.

rulebook.rule: Nominal is not real. Divide by inflation before you celebrate.
rulebook.why: Money is a rubber ruler. A raise below inflation is a pay cut.

rulebook.rule: Measure what matters in hours of work.
rulebook.why: Hours sidestep the moving ruler and show what is really getting cheaper or dearer.

rulebook.rule: Watch asset prices, not only consumer prices.
rulebook.why: The price of entering ownership can run far ahead of pay while headline inflation looks calm.

rulebook.rule: Own something productive from your first paycheck.
rulebook.why: Ownership compounds while you sleep. Wages stop when you stop.

rulebook.rule: Keep idle cash where it earns the safe rate.
rulebook.why: Banks and token issuers keep the gap between what safe bills pay and what they pay you.

rulebook.rule: No asset is safe in every season. Spread your bets across seasons, not just across names.
rulebook.why: Cash failed in the 1970s, long bonds failed from 2020 to 2023, stocks failed from 1929 to 1932.

rulebook.rule: Gold is insurance against the system, not income.
rulebook.why: It pays nothing and can fall for twenty years, but it shines when trust in money breaks.

rulebook.rule: When rulers need money they cannot raise honestly, they water down the currency.
rulebook.why: From Rome's denarius to modern inflation, debasement is the oldest hidden tax.

rulebook.rule: A temporary suspension of a money promise often becomes permanent.
rulebook.why: The 1971 gold suspension was announced as temporary and never ended.

rulebook.rule: Reserves held in someone else's currency come with someone else's conditions.
rulebook.why: Russia's frozen reserves in 2022 taught every government this rule.

rulebook.rule: Every trade deficit is also a capital inflow. Follow the dollars both ways.
rulebook.why: Cheap imports and cheap loans are two halves of the same loop, and someone pays for each.

rulebook.rule: Calm years breed risky borrowing. Be most careful when lending feels safest.
rulebook.why: Minsky showed that stability itself pushes people toward fragile debt.

rulebook.rule: When everyone repays at once, money shrinks. Keep a cash buffer for that day.
rulebook.why: Fisher showed that mass repayment can make debts heavier, so liquidity matters most when it is scarcest.

rulebook.rule: Watch interest against defense, and debt against output.
rulebook.why: These ratios have signaled decline in past empires, and interest now exceeds US defense spending.

rulebook.rule: New rails, old anchors. Ask what sits under any new money and who earns the interest.
rulebook.why: Stablecoins look new but are backed by Treasury bills, and the issuer keeps the yield.

rulebook.rule: Find the toll booths, and where you can, own one.
rulebook.why: Owners of crossing points, platforms, land and payment rails earn whether players win or lose.

rulebook.rule: Expect any fixed money promise to bend in a great war or crisis.
rulebook.why: Gold promises were suspended in 1914, 1933 and 1971.

rulebook.rule: Stop inflation early. Inflation people expect is far harder to stop than inflation that surprises.
rulebook.why: The 1970s show what happens when expectations take root, and Volcker shows the price of uprooting them.

rulebook.rule: Judge any plan to open the board by whether it gives real assets or credentials at scale.
rulebook.why: The Homestead Act and the GI Bill worked because they gave land, schooling and loan guarantees large enough to matter.

rulebook.rule: Separate the story from the mechanism. A ratio that only works today is a coincidence.
rulebook.why: The barter myth and the gold times ten idea both sound right and fail the test of history.

rulebook.rule: Check big decisions with more than one ruler: dollars, real dollars, hours and a hard asset.
rulebook.why: Every ruler moves. Agreement across several rulers is the closest thing to truth.

rulebook.rule: Pass on the mistakes, not just the successes.
rulebook.why: Each generation forgets its parents' crisis. Written lessons are the cheapest inheritance.

rulebook.rule: A crash headline is a repricing, not a robbery. Ask who was forced to sell, not who stole the value.
rulebook.why: Most lost market value was never cash, and forced sellers are what turn a dip into a crash.

rulebook.rule: Before you buy into a bucket, ask what is moving money into it and what would move it out.
rulebook.why: Rotation, not circulation, decides prices in the medium run.

rulebook.rule: Learn the bond before you trust any story about money.
rulebook.why: Rates, mortgages, stablecoins and currency power all rest on government bonds.

rulebook.rule: Ask who pays for a country's surplus, not just who earns it.
rulebook.why: Cheap currencies and exported savings move costs onto households.

rulebook.rule: Respect the bond market. It votes every second.
rulebook.why: Governments that lose its trust pay for it in higher interest bills.

rulebook.rule: Spend the melting money, keep the growing one, and know which is which.
rulebook.why: Gresham's law decides which money people spend and which they save.

rulebook.rule: Know which ruler your future spending will use.
rulebook.why: Savings that look safe in the home currency can shrink in the currency your future bills are priced in.

rulebook.rule: Follow where new money lands first.
rulebook.why: Hubs receive it early and at full value. Talent and capital follow.

rulebook.rule: Wealth on paper is a price, not a pile.
rulebook.why: Most wealth is the last trade's price on existing assets at today's interest rates. It cannot all be sold at that price.

rulebook.rule: Look for the next base layer before it is titled.
rulebook.why: Newcomers get ownership early only at new frontiers: new industries, energy, compute and whatever comes next.

rulebook.rule: The longer the bond, the bigger the swing.
rulebook.why: Long bonds lock in rent for more years, so their prices move most when rates change.

rulebook.rule: Money is debt. Know who owes the other side of every dollar you hold.
rulebook.why: Deposits, notes and bonds are all someone's liability. Only real things and gold or Bitcoin sit outside the mirror.

rulebook.rule: Tax is the subscription fee for the board. Argue about the size and who pays, not whether.
rulebook.why: Without the state there is no common money, no title and no court.

rulebook.rule: A yield is nominal. Subtract tax and inflation before you call it a gain.
rulebook.why: Bonds can pay every coupon on time and still lose buying power.

rulebook.rule: Geography deals the cards. Institutions decide whether a country can play them.
rulebook.why: Resource-rich countries with weak institutions often stay poor while refiners and financiers capture the value.

rulebook.rule: Crypto is three families, not one. Know which one you hold.
rulebook.why: Bitcoin, stablecoins and other tokens answer every money question differently.

rulebook.rule: If you cannot say where a yield comes from, the yield is the product being sold.
rulebook.why: Terra's 20% and many schemes since were paid from reserves or newer money, not earnings.

rulebook.rule: The ruler belongs to whatever debts and taxes are written in.
rulebook.why: Until wages, rents, mortgages and taxes are written in a token, every token gets converted to dollars somewhere.

rulebook.rule: Launching a token is printing money. Ask who pays for it.
rulebook.why: Unless a network earns real fees, the founders' seigniorage is paid by later buyers.

rulebook.rule: Money is not only made by bank loans. Ask which floor it lands on.
rulebook.why: Fed purchases and Treasury moves change reserves upstairs. Only some of them reach the deposits people can spend.

rulebook.rule: When the Fed buys bonds, look at who sold them.
rulebook.why: From a bank, only reserves rise. From a pension fund or other nonbank, a new public deposit appears too.

rulebook.rule: Banks are the everyday printer. The government plus the Fed is the emergency printer.
rulebook.why: Bank-loan money disappears when loans are repaid. Deficit money held by the Fed and banks tends to stay, because the debt is rolled over.

mistakes.mistake: Paid for armies by debasing the silver coin, then tried to stop the resulting price surge with a price edict in 301 AD.
mistakes.lesson: Price controls cannot hold back a watered-down money. Goods simply disappear from markets.

mistakes.mistake: Kept money fixed to gold while the economy grew, so prices fell for two decades and debtors, mostly farmers, were crushed.
mistakes.lesson: A money that cannot grow with the economy punishes borrowers, and its supply should not depend on mining luck.

mistakes.mistake: Bought stocks with borrowed money, often putting down a small fraction of the price, in the belief that prosperity was permanent.
mistakes.lesson: Leverage plus euphoria produces forced selling. When prices turn, borrowed money must still be repaid.

mistakes.mistake: Let thousands of banks fail, allowed the money supply to shrink by about a third, clung to the gold standard and raised tariffs.
mistakes.lesson: In a panic, the central bank must lend freely against good collateral. Countries that left gold earlier recovered sooner.

mistakes.mistake: Paid for war and new programs at once while promising gold at $35, ignoring the Triffin warning.
mistakes.lesson: A promise that must keep growing will eventually outgrow what backs it. Plan the exit before the run.

mistakes.mistake: Treated inflation as a small price for jobs, tried wage and price controls, and tightened only briefly before easing again.
mistakes.lesson: Once people expect inflation, it feeds itself. Stopping it late costs far more than stopping it early.

mistakes.generation: Latin American borrowers and their lenders, around 1980
mistakes.mistake: Recycled oil dollars into loans at floating interest rates in a currency the borrowers could not print.
mistakes.lesson: Borrowing in someone else's currency at floating rates hands your fate to their central bank.

mistakes.mistake: Let banks hide bad loans and kept failing firms alive, so the economy repaired its balance sheets slowly for decades.
mistakes.lesson: Recognize losses quickly and recapitalize banks. Slow cleanup turns a bust into a lost generation.

mistakes.mistake: Believed house prices could not fall nationwide, lent to borrowers who could not repay and stacked leverage on top.
mistakes.lesson: Housing is not risk-free. Stability bred the fragile debt that Minsky warned about.

mistakes.mistake: Assumed near-zero interest rates would last and loaded up on long-term bonds and cheap fixed debt for assets.
mistakes.lesson: Safe assets are safe only in a season. When rates rose, banks like Silicon Valley Bank failed holding them.

mistakes.mistake: Called the inflation surge transitory for too long, and chased high crypto yields from lenders that re-lent customer assets.
mistakes.lesson: Every yield has a source. If you cannot see where the return comes from, you may be the return.

A city where money, banks, investors and talent concentrate, such as New York, London or Singapore.
Keeping interest rates below inflation so that debts, especially government debts, shrink in real terms.
A currency whose price against others is set by markets every day.
Walter Scheidel's name for the four forces that historically shrank inequality: mass-mobilization war, revolution, state collapse and pandemics.

A system where a currency is defined as a fixed weight of gold and paper notes can be swapped for gold.

The cut in Bitcoin's new-coin reward about every four years. The April 2024 halving set it at 3.125 coins per block.

The fiftieth-year release in Leviticus 25, when land returned to its original families and bonded servants went free. The release of debts every seventh year comes from Deuteronomy 15.

Something you owe, such as a loan. One person's liability is always another's asset.
The date a bond repays its face value.
Whatever people hand over to settle a trade. Money's spending job.
A token with no purpose beyond attention and speculation.
When a country grows fast to a middle level and then stalls, often because the next step needs reforms its elites resist.

The Fed buying or selling securities in the market, with dealers, rather than directly from the Treasury.
A fixed exchange rate between one currency and another, defended by a central bank.
The 1970s arrangement in which oil was priced in dollars and Gulf oil money was recycled into US Treasuries and banks.
One of 25 banks and dealers that must bid at US Treasury auctions and trade with the New York Fed in its open market operations.
The government's deficit before counting interest payments.
A game where each player gains by cheating, but if all cheat, all end up worse off.
The secret code that controls tokens in a wallet. Whoever holds it controls the tokens.
A compulsory national savings scheme for retirement, such as Malaysia's EPF or Singapore's CPF.
When a central bank creates reserves to buy bonds in the open market, to push down long-term interest rates.
Adjusted for inflation, so values can be compared across time.
The return left after inflation. In bond markets it is read from inflation-protected bonds (TIPS).
A short loan backed by bonds as collateral. The financial system's overnight pawnshop.
A currency that foreign governments hold in large amounts as savings and for crisis use. Today mainly the dollar.
The pattern where countries rich in oil or minerals grow slower and govern worse than countries without them.
A change in the price of assets already owned, with no new things produced. Falling interest rates revalue assets upward.
A Fed facility where money funds and others park cash overnight, taking it out of the banking system while it sits there.
The Arabic term for interest or unjust gain on loans, forbidden in Islam.
The profit from issuing money, the gap between what money costs to make and what it buys.
A state-owned fund that invests a country's surplus, often from oil, gas or trade, in assets at home and abroad.
A crypto token designed to stay worth one unit of a currency, usually one dollar, backed by reserves.
A way to carry buying power from today into the future. Money's saving job.
Islamic bonds that pay returns linked to real assets instead of interest.
Countries cutting taxes to attract people, companies and capital from other countries.
The extra yield investors demand for locking money up for many years when the future is uncertain.
The fact that people value having things sooner rather than later. It is why waiting must be paid for with interest.
The number of hours of work needed to buy something.
The legal record of who owns something, such as land, a building or mineral rights.
A unit recorded on a blockchain. It can represent a coin, a dollar, a share, a vote or nothing at all.
Recording ownership of a real asset, such as a Treasury bill or a building, on a blockchain.

The US government's main checking account, held at the Federal Reserve.
Debts of the US government. Bills last up to a year, notes 2 to 10 years, bonds 20 or 30 years.
The conflict between supplying the world with enough of a reserve currency and keeping that currency's backing believable.
The measuring unit for prices, wages and debts, such as the dollar. Money's measuring job.
How many times a unit of money is spent in a given period.
This project's name for dollar loans backed by energy assets such as power plants, data centers and chips.
The return on a bond or investment, expressed as a yearly percentage of its price.

questions.q: If the market drops 20%, did someone else make that money?
questions.a: Mostly no. Market cap is the last price times all shares, so a fall rewrites the value of every share even though only a few traded. Sellers received cash from buyers. Only short sellers and option buyers profit from the fall, and only by what their direct counterparties lose. See chapter 19.

questions.q: If the government can create money, why does it borrow and tax at all?
questions.a: Taxes give money its demand and keep spending from overheating the economy. Borrowing lets the government spend more than it taxes without the central bank directly creating new money for it, which the law restricts. If a government simply created money for all its spending, inflation would follow, as many countries have shown.

questions.q: Why not just print enough money to pay off the national debt?
questions.a: The money would flood into the economy and push prices up, eroding everyone's savings. Also, much of the debt is held as savings by pension funds, banks and families, so paying it off with new money would turn their safe assets into cash during an inflation.

questions.q: Is the dollar going to collapse?
questions.a: Nobody can promise anything, but this project's October 2026 view gives the dollar system about a 62% chance of continuing to extend its role through 2028, with the chance of a disorderly reset rising over longer horizons. Currencies at the top usually decline slowly, over decades, not overnight.

questions.q: Is my money safe in the bank?
questions.a: In the United States, deposits are insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category. Below that limit, your deposit is very safe. Above it, you are trusting the bank's own finances.

questions.q: Should I buy gold?
questions.a: This guide is not financial advice. Gold is best understood as insurance against a loss of trust in money and its managers. It pays no income and can fall for long stretches, as it did from 1980 to 2001. Many people who hold it keep it as a modest slice, not their whole savings.

questions.q: Is Bitcoin money?
questions.a: It works as a medium of exchange in some places and as a store of value for some holders, but it is too volatile to be a good unit of account. Today it acts mostly as an asset held outside the banking system, not as everyday money.

questions.q: Why does inflation exist at all? Could we have zero?
questions.a: Most central banks aim for about 2% because mild inflation makes wage adjustments easier, leaves room to cut rates and keeps the economy away from deflation traps. Zero is possible but risky, because a small shock can tip it into deflation.

questions.q: Who decides interest rates?
questions.a: The Fed sets a short-term rate for overnight lending between banks. Longer-term rates, such as mortgage rates, are set by markets based on inflation expectations, government borrowing and demand for safe assets.

questions.q: Why does the US have so much debt and still borrow cheaply?
questions.a: Because the world needs dollars and safe dollar assets, US Treasuries have a large built-in demand. That demand is not unlimited, which is why yields rose in 2026 as debt grew and some foreign buyers sold.

questions.q: What happens if China sells all its Treasuries?
questions.a: Yields would rise and the dollar might weaken, but China would also lose money on its sales and push up its own currency, hurting its exports. This project rates a fire sale as very unlikely. China has instead reduced its holdings gradually, from about $694 billion in February 2026 to about $591 billion in August.

questions.q: Will stablecoins replace banks?
questions.a: They are replacing some ways money moves, not the lending that banks do. Stablecoins cannot lend or pay interest by law, and they are backed by Treasury bills. Loans against your future income still come from regulated lenders.

questions.q: Can the US just revalue its gold to pay the debt?
questions.a: Revaluing its gold to market price would book about $1.07 trillion, roughly one year of net interest, once. The deficit recurs every year, so it would not solve the problem.

questions.q: If interest is never created, how can all loans be repaid?
questions.a: Interest is paid out of money that circulates. When lenders spend their interest income, it returns to borrowers through wages and sales. The real risk is debt growing faster than incomes, or everyone trying to repay at the same moment.

questions.q: Why do house prices rise faster than inflation?
questions.a: House prices are mostly land prices in expensive cities, and land cannot be made. Low interest rates, limited building and zoning rules push prices up, while the consumer price index counts rents, not purchase prices.

questions.q: Will AI and robots make everything free?
questions.a: They are already making many goods cheaper in hours of work. But housing, land, health care and attention are not getting cheaper, and this project's research found that robots can meet only part of any extra demand while housing supply grows about 1% a year.

questions.q: What is the single most useful habit from this guide?
questions.a: Own something productive from your first paycheck, and borrow only what you can carry through a bad season. Those two rules protect you in almost every season of money.

questions.q: Why do bond prices fall when interest rates rise?
questions.a: A bond's payments are fixed. When new bonds pay more, an old bond only sells if its price drops until its fixed payments give the same yield. See the bonds chapter.

questions.q: Why does China or Japan lend so much to the US instead of spending it at home?
questions.a: To keep their currencies cheap for exporters, to hold insurance against a dollar shortage, and because US markets are deeper and safer than their own. Their households pay part of the cost. See the leaderboard chapter.

questions.q: If a money gains value over time, why would anyone spend it?
questions.a: People still need things now, and waiting has a cost. In practice they spend the money that is losing value and keep the one that is gaining, which is Gresham's law. See the deflation debate chapter.

questions.q: My local inflation is low. Why do I feel poorer when I travel or pay overseas fees?
questions.a: Because your home currency may have weakened against the currencies those bills are priced in. Low home inflation measures only the home ruler. See the chapter on the view from a smaller currency.

questions.q: If the world is so rich, why do so many people feel locked out?
questions.a: Because most of that wealth is the price of assets that were owned long ago, revalued upward by falling interest rates, while newcomers must buy in at today's prices with credit. See the chapter on the titled world.

questions.q: Is tax a scam?
questions.a: No. Tax is the fee for the board itself: the money, the courts that protect your title and the security around them. But who pays the fee and how well it is spent are fair questions. See the Nation Inc. chapter.

questions.q: Why do bond prices fall when rates rise? I still find it confusing.
questions.a: Picture an apartment with a locked rent. If rents in town rise, a buyer will not pay full price for your low locked rent. A bond's coupon is that locked rent. Try the slider in the bonds chapter.

questions.q: If my bond pays 5%, am I really 5% richer each year?
questions.a: No. 5% is the nominal yield. Take off tax and inflation and the real gain may be closer to 1% or 2%, or even below zero. Try the second slider in the bonds chapter.

questions.q: Why are countries full of minerals often poor?
questions.a: Because the value is mostly captured at the refining, manufacturing and financial steps, and because easy resource money weakens institutions. See the geography section of the leaderboard chapter.

questions.q: Is crypto money?
questions.a: It depends on the family. Stablecoins work as money but are really dollars. Bitcoin is a candidate store of value but is rarely spent or used to price things. Most other tokens are not money at all. See the crypto chapter and its six questions.

questions.q: If tokens get good enough, will we still need the dollar to measure prices?
questions.a: Only if debts, wages and taxes start being written in a token. Until then every token is converted to dollars somewhere along the chain, and markets keep rebuilding one hub to price everything through. See the owner's question in the crypto chapter.

questions.q: Is money only created when banks make loans?
questions.a: No. Banks also create deposits when they buy securities, the Fed creates them when it buys from nonbanks, and Treasury spending adds them while taxes and auctions take them away. See the chapter on who really creates money.
